newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges new Zaire leader move toward elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges new Zaire leader move toward elections.

text.p: The United States on Saturday welcomed what it called a relatively smooth transfer of power in Zaire and urged the new leadership to establish an inclusive transitional government leading to elections.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila proclaimed himself head of state of Zaire on Saturday as his forces entered the capital Kinshasa virtually unopposed and the army of departed President Mobutu Sese Seko switched sides or fled.
"The United States welcomes reports that the transfer of power in Kinshasa is occurring with only minimal disorder and unrest," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

"This is an historic opportunity to shape the future of the country. We call on the new leadership to establish an inclusive transitional government leading to elections, and to ensure full respect for human rights throughout the country," he said.

After backing Mobutu for decades as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism, the United States and other Western states in recent weeks withdrew their support and wielded their influence to persuade him to step aside.

But administration officials and foreign policy experts said it was still too early to tell what sort of government Kabila would set up, and how long it would take until the people of Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, would finally see democratic elections.
One of Kabila's first acts was to revert to the name Zaire had on independence from Belgium in 1960 until Mobutu changed it in 1971.

State Department spokeswoman Sharon Bowman could not confirm a report on Zairean rebel radio that the United States and the European Union have pledged $60 million to Kabila to help him organise elections as soon as he takes power.
"The nature of our relationship with the new authorities will depend upon their commitment to democratic reforms, public accountability and respect for human rights," she said.

Kabila, Mobuto's opponent for more than 30 years, said he would set up a transitional government of public salvation within 72 hours and told Mobutu's army to lay down its arms and also pledged a constituent assembly within 60 days to work out a new transitional constitution.
But he did not mention the democratic elections he called for in the early days of his revolt, which mushroomed from an October dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis.

"It's so early in the game, we don't even know what the new government is going to look like," said one administration official, expressing some concern over the country's new name, which carries certain Marxist connotations.

Elliott Skinner, a former U.S. ambassador to Burkina Faso now an anthropology professor at Columbia University, said Kabila would likely try to stay in power for some time and holding early elections might actually support the political power structures erected by Mobuto.

"While I think it's important to talk about ultimately moving toward democracy, the factors on the ground might dictate that we give the government an opportunity to craft a new political system," Skinner told Reuters.

Carol Lancaster, professor at Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service, said it was unclear how much leverage Washington and its allies would have with Kabila, especially in light of reports that Western business interests are already wooing him with lucrative mining contracts.

"It's not at all clear that Kaliba is a democrat; he may well find it irrestible to retain power," she said. "The thing that may make that more attractive is that businessmen are already seeking contracts with his government. I'm not sure how much leverage the United States has at this point."
The State Department on Saturday also said it had no immediate plans to evacuate the 25 personnel at the U.S. embassy and 310 private Americans still in the country.
"We're not expecting to do that as of now," said spokeswoman Bowman.
